This is the name Anil Seth gives to the assumption underlying every claim that AI could be conscious. As the passage puts it, the idea is that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth stresses that this is a philosophical position, not a settled fact: this assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all. But that is what it is. And the stakes of the whole essay hinge on it: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with.

This term also sits at the head of the essay's next major section, where Seth distinguishes it from the broader, less controversial idea of "functionalism" in philosophy of mind (roughly, that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization). Computational functionalism is the narrower, stronger claim that the relevant organization is specifically computational — and, in most versions, computational in the Turing-machine sense he goes on to dissect. The four arguments that follow in the article (that brains aren't computers, that other non-computational dynamics may matter, that biological life itself may be necessary, and that simulation isn't instantiation) are all aimed at this one target: showing why it's much less obviously true than its ubiquity in AI discourse suggests.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This is naming the assumption Seth has just introduced in the sentence right before: that consciousness arises simply from running the right kind of computation or information processing. He is not yet arguing against it here — this line is just labelling it and flagging why it goes unnoticed.

The term "computational functionalism" comes from philosophy of mind. Functionalism in general is the view that mental states are defined by what they do — their causal role, their inputs and outputs — rather than by what they are made of. Computational functionalism narrows that further: it says the specific kind of functional organization that produces a mind is computational, and (as Seth uses it here) usually means computation in Turing's sense — the standard notion of algorithmic, digital computation running on any suitable hardware. On this view, if a system carries out the right program, it doesn't matter whether that program runs on neurons, silicon, or anything else; consciousness would follow automatically.

Seth's point in this sentence is about why the assumption is hard to see as an assumption at all: it sits quietly underneath the whole idea of conscious AI, so naturally that people treat it as just an obvious fact about minds rather than a contestable philosophical claim. That is exactly the move he is setting up to challenge — the rest of this section goes on to lay out four related arguments that undermine the idea that computation, at least of the sort implemented in standard digital computers, is sufficient for consciousness. So this sentence is the hinge: having named the hidden assumption, Seth spends the following pages trying to make it visible and then dismantle it.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the assumption, as the article puts it, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth stresses that this is not a proven fact but an unexamined premise: this assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all. But that is what it is [spya-wepmnr].

It matters to the whole essay because Seth treats it as the load-bearing premise under every claim that AI could be conscious: the very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation, and he says plainly that if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The four arguments that follow — brains aren't computers, other non-computational dynamics may matter, life itself may be necessary, and simulation isn't instantiation — are all built to chip away at this one assumption [spya-cv97j7 spya-sk4su6 spya-affgsh spya-e7jqx4 spya-cqh5wq]. He makes the stakes explicit near the end when summarizing: Computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn]. It also surfaces later as the hidden premise inside other ideas he criticizes, such as whole-brain emulation and Bostrom's simulation hypothesis: the prospect of instantiating consciousness through some kind of whole-brain emulation, at some arbitrarily high level of detail, already assumes that computational functionalism is true, and it is telling that he notes one necessary assumption, and then just takes it as a given. This, perhaps unsurprisingly, is the assumption that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-pbcr03 spya-xdy4fe].

So structurally, the term names the single claim Seth thinks the whole "conscious AI is coming" story depends on, and his essay's central move is to make that claim visible and then argue, piece by piece, that it is far less secure than people assume.

Autopoiesis is the term Seth borrows here to name something about living cells specifically: the fact that even a single neuron is, as the passage puts it, "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." The word itself comes from Greek, and Seth glosses it directly: "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.'" He then adds his own assessment of its significance: "Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems."

The point of introducing it here is to sharpen the contrast he's building between brains and computers. A computer chip doesn't rebuild itself out of its own ongoing activity — it just executes instructions on fixed hardware. A living cell, by contrast, is constantly using its own processes to remake the very physical stuff that makes it what it is; its "doing" and its "being" are tangled together in a way a machine's aren't. This sets up the argument a few paragraphs later that brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to cleanly separate what they do from what they are — which is precisely the separation (between software and hardware) that makes the brain-as-computer metaphor work in the first place.

Although the article doesn't elaborate on its origin, autopoiesis is a concept originally developed in the 1970s by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to define what distinguishes living systems from non-living ones — the idea that a living thing is a network of processes that continuously produces and repairs the very components (like cell membranes) that produce those processes. Seth is drawing on that established biological/philosophical concept to argue that this self-producing quality of life may be relevant to consciousness in a way no silicon computer could replicate, since silicon doesn't sustain itself through anything analogous to metabolism.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a term coined in the early 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to describe what makes something alive in the first place. The word combines the Greek for "self" and "production" (as the article notes), and it names a system that continuously builds and repairs its own parts and its own boundary from the inside, rather than being built or maintained by something external. A cell is the classic example: its membrane, proteins and internal machinery are all made and remade by the cell's own ongoing chemistry, so the thing and the process that keeps it going are the same thing.

In the passage, the article uses this idea to make a point about brains specifically: it says a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence, and glosses this self-maintaining activity as autopoiesis, calling it arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems. The move here is to distinguish a neuron from a silicon component in a computer chip: a transistor just sits there switching states as designed, but a neuron is constantly rebuilding itself as part of what it does. This sets up the essay's later argument (in the section on "Life Matters") that this self-producing, self-sustaining character of living tissue may be inseparable from what makes consciousness possible at all — which is part of why Seth doubts that a silicon system, lacking anything like autopoiesis, could ever host the same thing.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the piece, autopoiesis is the term for a living thing's continuous self-maintenance: a single neuron is described as "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," and the text adds, "This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for 'self-production.' Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" [spya-cf8rt8].

It does two jobs in the argument. First, in the "Brains Are Not Computers" section, it's evidence that a brain isn't cleanly split into software and hardware the way a computer is — the brain's material keeps regenerating itself rather than sitting still as neutral "wetware" running separate "mindware," which is part of why the author says there's no reason to expect the sharp software/hardware separation Turing computation relies on [spya-cf8rt8 spya-zw2m7u spya-ycpfzs].

Second, it resurfaces in the "Life Matters" section (argument 3, biological naturalism), where the drive to stay alive is traced down into the cell's metabolism, and the author draws what he calls "a mathematical line… directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self" [spya-vys3vj]. So autopoiesis is the hinge connecting "brains aren't computers" to "life itself, not just information processing, may be what consciousness needs" — it's offered as one reason the material, living substrate can't be swapped out for silicon without losing something essential [spya-da9tvt].
